articles.headline: El 'Gran Hermano' de los incendios ya vigila Lugo las 24 horas
articles.subtitle: La sala de control de la Rede de Vixilancia forestal de la Xunta opera desde la delegación de Lugo con 64 cámaras de 360 grados, cuatro helicópteros, drones y un teléfono único, en un despliegue que ha evolucionado tras los grandes incendios de los últimos años.
articles.body:
La Xunta vigila los montes de Lugo las 24 horas desde una sala situada en la delegación territorial de la capital, en la Ronda da Muralla, donde la Rede de Vixilancia de Espazos Forestais concentra las imágenes de 64 cámaras de 360 grados, cuatro de ellas instaladas en helicópteros, y la información que aportan los drones y las llamadas al teléfono único 085 y a la aplicación ALume.

El responsable de prevención y extinción en Lugo, Ignacio Sánchez, explica que el sistema nació hace dos décadas, cuando Galicia era la pira de Europa, y que hoy la inteligencia artificial ayuda a diseñar rutas y a analizar lo que captan las cámaras. La provincia estrenará seis nuevos puntos de vigilancia en Láncara, O Valadouro, A Fonsagrada, Becerreá, Portomarín y Sober.

El despliegue se completa con los equipos Batracio, de quince personas, y con contratos de limpieza de rozas que este año suman 25 millones de euros, a los que se añaden otros seis millones para mejorar las condiciones laborales del operativo, en un verano en el que los incendios de sexta generación, con una radiación de hasta 80.000 kilovatios, han vuelto a marcar la campaña.

articles.headline: Descubren en Pastoriza una mina de oro romana de 117 hectáreas
articles.subtitle: El yacimiento, hallado en Campo do Oso durante una prospección arqueológica vinculada a un proyecto minero, conserva los canales que permitían extraer el oro por fuerza hidráulica y podría dinamizar la actividad cultural de la comarca.
articles.body:
Un yacimiento aurífero del siglo I antes de Cristo, con una superficie estimada de más de 117 hectáreas, ha sido localizado en Campo do Oso, en el municipio de Pastoriza, durante unos trabajos de investigación arqueológica ligados a la ampliación de una mina en el propio concello. El arqueólogo Francisco Hervés, encargado de la prospección superficial intensiva, creyó en un primer momento haber encontrado un campamento militar romano.

Lo más singular del hallazgo es la conservación de los canales por los que el agua descendía con fuerza para arrastrar los sedimentos del interior de la montaña hasta unas balsas donde, mediante bateo, se obtenía el oro. Al tratarse de una explotación del Estado, era el propio emperador quien encargaba fiscalizar la producción, destinada sobre todo a la acuñación de monedas y a piezas de prestigio.

Hervés defiende que el yacimiento, comparable en atractivo al castro de Viladonga, podría potenciar la actividad cultural de la zona y servir para divulgar el impacto de Roma en Galicia, y pide que se cataloguen las explotaciones auríferas de la comarca antes de que grandes proyectos acaben destruyéndolas.

articles.headline: Muere un militar de la UME en el incendio de Las Peñas de Riglos
articles.subtitle: El camión autobomba en el que viajaba volcó y cayó por un barranco en Huesca; otros tres militares resultaron heridos, uno de ellos trasladado al hospital Miguel Servet de Zaragoza, mientras el fuego supera las 17.500 hectáreas.
articles.body:
Un militar de la Unidad Militar de Emergencias falleció este domingo al volcar el camión autobomba en el que viajaba durante las labores de extinción del incendio de Las Peñas de Riglos, en Huesca. El vehículo se despeñó en el barranco de Atarés, junto al monte Oroel, y otros tres militares resultaron heridos: dos fueron atendidos en el hospital de Jaca y un tercero, en estado estable, fue trasladado al Miguel Servet de Zaragoza.

El siniestro se produjo en el marco del dispositivo desplegado contra un fuego que ya supera las 17.500 hectáreas, con cerca de un millar de efectivos y más de cuarenta medios aéreos, y que mantiene evacuadas a 1.046 personas de 19 poblaciones y tres campamentos. El comité de dirección, reunido a las ocho de la tarde, guardó un minuto de silencio por el militar fallecido.

La noche fue más favorable, con humedad y menos viento, y este lunes se incorporan un centenar de bomberos franceses llegados a través del mecanismo de protección civil de la Unión Europea. Las condolencias por el fallecido se sucedieron a lo largo de la jornada, desde el presidente del Gobierno hasta el del Ejecutivo aragonés, mientras el presunto autor del incendio permanece en prisión provisional.

articles.headline: Cientos de migrantes reclaman su derecho de asilo en Ceuta: 'No queremos volver a Marruecos'
articles.subtitle: Unos doscientos migrantes del asentamiento de la playa del Trampolín se concentran para exigir asilo en España, entre 5.000 y 8.000 personas permanecen en la ciudad tras la entrada masiva del 30 de julio y el Gobierno descarta el colapso sanitario.
articles.body:
Unos doscientos migrantes que permanecen en el asentamiento improvisado de la playa del Trampolín, en Ceuta, protagonizaron este domingo una concentración para reclamar su derecho de asilo, con pancartas en las que se leían mensajes como 'No queremos volver a Marruecos' o 'También somos humanos' y cánticos de 'Estamos cansados'.

Mohammed Ouanzar, un especialista en automatización de 39 años originario de Fez, aseguró que prefiere morir antes que regresar, porque con sueldos medios de unos 280 euros al mes es imposible formar una familia. Emmanuel, un electricista nigeriano de 30 años que huyó del conflicto del noreste de su país tras un viaje de cuatro meses, dijo que lucha por una vida mejor para sus hijos.

Entre 5.000 y 8.000 personas permanecen en Ceuta desde la entrada masiva del 30 de julio, cuando más de 72.000 irrumpieron en la ciudad y la mayoría regresó en los días siguientes. El ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, insiste en que ninguna persona que entró de forma irregular se quedará ni viajará a la península.

articles.headline: Interior instala una barrera flotante en el dique sur de Melilla, como en Ceuta
articles.subtitle: El dispositivo de contención, colocado en el mar al final del espigón de 500 metros que separa la ciudad del puerto marroquí de Nador, se suma a las vallas levantadas la semana pasada y busca dar seguridad jurídica a los rechazos en la frontera marítima.
articles.body:
El Ministerio del Interior ha instalado una barrera flotante en el mar al final del dique sur de Melilla, un espigón de 500 metros que separa la ciudad autónoma del puerto marroquí de Nador, en un dispositivo similar al desplegado en Ceuta, según confirmó EFE. El dique quedó cerrado al tráfico tras los trabajos.

La barrera se suma a las vallas de obra colocadas la semana pasada en el tramo final del espigón, una medida adoptada después de que el Tribunal Supremo impidiera los rechazos en caliente de quienes entran a nado. La Secretaría de Estado de Seguridad ha instruido a las fuerzas para dar seguridad jurídica a la actuación en la línea marítima.

La delegada del Gobierno en Melilla, Sabrina Moh, defendió que los elementos instalados están adaptados a la realidad de la frontera. Fuentes de Interior citadas por la agencia Reuters describen la barrera como una solución temporal y provisional para el rechazo de migrantes.

articles.headline: El incendio de Niebla queda estabilizado y todos los evacuados vuelven a casa
articles.subtitle: Tras diez días, el fuego más extenso de la historia de Andalucía, con más de 38.000 hectáreas afectadas, queda estabilizado y 417 personas de once municipios regresan a sus viviendas, mientras la UME abandona la zona entre aplausos.
articles.body:
El incendio forestal de Niebla, en Huelva, quedó estabilizado este domingo a las diez y media de la mañana, según anunció el presidente andaluz, Juanma Moreno, desde el puesto de mando avanzado. Con un perímetro de 210 kilómetros y más de 38.000 hectáreas afectadas, es el incendio más extenso de la historia de Andalucía y los trabajos pasaron a nivel operativo uno.

Las 417 personas de once municipios que permanecían desalojadas comenzaron a regresar a sus viviendas, y la Unidad Militar de Emergencias abandonó la zona entre aplausos de los vecinos después de diez días de lucha contra el fuego, que llegó a entrar en la provincia de Sevilla por Aznalcóllar.

Mientras tanto, el incendio de Las Peñas de Riglos, en Huesca, vivió una noche tranquila gracias a la humedad y al poco viento, con más de mil efectivos y la llegada de un centenar de bomberos franceses, y el fuego de Hermisende, en Zamora, mejoró hasta el punto de rebajar el nivel de alerta.

articles.headline: Inside Derry's 'forgotten' republican heartlands as bonfires burn
articles.subtitle: A week after almost 500 pallets were seized from beneath the Lecky Road flyover, the Bogside and Creggan rebuilt their August 15 pyres, held self-funded family fun days and lit the bonfires as a protest, as police treat the night's events as sectarian hate crimes.
articles.body:
A week after a dawn raid in which contractors seized almost 500 pallets from beneath Derry's Lecky Road flyover, republican communities in the Bogside and Creggan rebuilt their August 15 bonfires and lit them in protest, surrounded by family fun days and crowds of onlookers. The pallets had been removed over fire safety fears linked to gas mains beneath the tarmac, a claim many residents said they found hard to believe.

Residents described the 15th as a family celebration and spoke of a city that feels left behind, comparing the summer festivals of Belfast with what they called the deprivation of the Bogside. A poster reading 'Sinn Féin sellouts' appeared on the pyre, prompting First Minister Michelle O'Neill to condemn the bonfires as a 'blight' and 'the very opposite of republicanism'.

Police are treating the burning of material at three bonfires across the city as sectarian-motivated hate crimes, with Chief Superintendent Gillian Kearney condemning what was placed on the pyres. The events came days after a flag bearing slogans against police was condemned across the political spectrum.

articles.headline: Veteran republican Gerry Kelly will not contest next Stormont election
articles.subtitle: The 73-year-old North Belfast MLA is stepping down after 30 years as an elected representative, telling the Irish News he will remain an activist 'just not a 24/7 activist' — tributes led by Sinn Féin follow.
articles.body:
Veteran republican Gerry Kelly has revealed that he will not stand in next year's Stormont election, bringing the curtain down on a political career spanning 30 years. The 73-year-old North Belfast MLA told the Irish News he would remain an activist, 'just not a 24/7 activist'.

His first venture into representative politics came as part of the Northern Ireland Forum in 1996, before he was elected to the Assembly after the Good Friday Agreement in 1998, making him one of its longest-serving members alongside Speaker Edwin Poots. Born in west Belfast, he joined Fianna Éireann in his teens and was arrested in 1971, spending time in Mountjoy Prison before escaping and returning to Belfast.

Sinn Féin paid tribute to a man it said had given 'a lifetime of service and commitment to the cause of Irish unity' and shown great leadership across North Belfast. His departure will be felt in the Assembly's republican benches as the party prepares for the next election campaign.

articles.headline: Martina Anderson reveals she had an abortion so IRA operation could go ahead
articles.subtitle: The former Sinn Féin MEP, who was 22 and on the run in 1985, says the decision 'broke me but I was not for letting my comrades down', and speaks of the social shaming of women who had abortions during the Troubles.
articles.body:
Former Sinn Féin MEP and Foyle MLA Martina Anderson has revealed that she underwent an abortion in 1985, aged 22, so that an IRA bombing mission she was preparing to join in England could go ahead. In an interview with RTÉ, she described it as the hardest and most painful decision of her life: 'It didn't strengthen me making that decision. In fact, it broke me but I was not for letting my comrades down.'

Anderson, who was on the run in the Republic when she discovered she was pregnant weeks into the planning of the unspecified attack, said she has 'lived in silence' about her ordeal for more than 40 years. She married fellow IRA prisoner Paul Kavanagh in Full Sutton Prison in 1989, and was ordered to stand aside from her seat by the Sinn Féin leadership in 2021.

She said she hoped that telling her story might help stop 'the social and moral shaming of women like me'. The former prisoner later described the reaction to her revelation as an 'onslaught of misogyny, hate, and social media attacks', while insisting there is no justification for dissident violence today.

articles.headline: Indonesia earthquake death toll rises past 47 as rescuers search for survivors
articles.subtitle: Rescuers in eastern Indonesia have recovered six more bodies after the magnitude 7.7 quake struck off Flores, toppling buildings and displacing thousands, with the toll expected to keep rising in the Labuan Bajo area.
articles.body:
Rescuers in Indonesia have recovered six more bodies from the aftermath of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake that struck off the island of Flores, as the known death toll reached at least 47, with more than 100 people injured and thousands displaced. The quake toppled buildings and triggered landslides across several districts of East Nusa Tenggara.

The hardest-hit areas include the tourist gateway of Labuan Bajo, the Komodo district and towns along the Trans-Flores highway, where families have been sleeping outside amid ongoing aftershocks. Rescue teams are struggling to reach some communities after roads were cut by landslides.

The earthquake is among the strongest to hit the region in years. In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 quake triggered a tsunami on Sulawesi that killed more than 4,400 people, while the 2004 Sumatra quake unleashed a tsunami that killed about 230,000 people across a dozen countries.

articles.headline: Russia launches massive overnight barrage across Ukraine as Kyiv strikes back with record drone wave
articles.subtitle: At least five people were killed as Russia hit eleven regions with missiles and drones, disconnecting Moldova's key power link, hours after Ukraine launched what Moscow said was its largest drone attack of the war, killing six in Russia.
articles.body:
Russia launched a massive overnight barrage of missiles and drones across Ukraine, killing at least five people and damaging infrastructure in eleven regions, according to Ukrainian officials. The Ukrainian Air Force said seven ballistic missiles, 23 cruise missiles, four air-launched guided missiles and 392 drones were used, with air defences intercepting 25 missiles and 365 drones.

A 61-year-old woman was killed when a drone hit an electric train in Kharkiv, while further deaths were reported in Zaporizhzhia, Kherson and Poltava. President Volodymyr Zelensky had warned hours earlier that intelligence pointed to a massive strike, and the barrage also disconnected Moldova's key power link with Europe, which President Maia Sandu said left the situation 'fragile'.

The attack came as Ukraine itself launched what Moscow described as one of the largest drone waves of the war, with 822 drones shot down, a fire at a Wildberries warehouse near Moscow and at least six people killed in Russia, in the biggest air raid on the Russian capital in two years.

articles.headline: Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon kill 11 in deadliest attacks since June truce
articles.subtitle: An air strike on a house in Ansar killed seven people, including three children and two women, and further strikes hit Deir al Zahrani, as Lebanese leaders condemned the escalation and the toll became the worst since the ceasefire framework.
articles.body:
Israeli strikes on southern Lebanon have killed at least 11 people, Lebanese authorities said, in the deadliest attacks since the June ceasefire framework. A strike on a house on the outskirts of Ansar at about 04:30 killed seven people, including three children and two women, in a building where displaced families were living, according to the state news agency.

A further round of strikes hit the town of Deir al Zahrani, killing two people and injuring nine. Prime Minister Nawaf Salam condemned the attacks, saying the civilians killed were not military infrastructure: 'Israel must halt this escalation,' he said, while President Joseph Aoun said the strikes sent a clear message to the US-led negotiations.

Israel's military said it had struck Hezbollah infrastructure in response to an earlier action against its soldiers near the Ali al-Taher Ridge, and the IDF said it would continue to remove threats in the occupied security zone. The June framework calls for Hezbollah to disarm and Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon.

articles.headline: Self-driving trucks are officially testing on California highways
articles.subtitle: Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI have received the first permits from the California DMV to test autonomous heavy-duty trucks on public roads, ending their home state's ban, with a human safety operator required behind the wheel.
articles.body:
Aurora Innovation and Kodiak AI have received permits from the California Department of Motor Vehicles to test their self-driving trucks on public roads, under rules approved in April that lifted the state's ban on autonomous vehicles weighing more than 10,000 pounds. Kodiak has already started with a handful of test trucks around its Mountain View office.

The permits require a human safety operator to be behind the wheel and prohibit testing on roads with speed limits of 25 mph or less unless on a direct route. Both companies had focused on Texas, where Aurora launched a commercial self-driving truck service in May 2025 and Kodiak has run driverless operations since January 2025.

Kodiak's founder, Don Burnette, called the permit 'a major unlock for freight innovation' and the first step toward scaling autonomous trucking coast-to-coast. The rollout faces opposition: Teamsters California sued the DMV last week, alleging the agency failed to study the economic and safety impacts of autonomous trucks.

articles.headline: US courts will start publishing how often the government uses spyware
articles.subtitle: For the first time, the federal judiciary will publicly count court-authorized wiretaps carried out with hacking tools and commercial spyware, starting with the 2028 Wiretap Report — a transparency win advocates have sought for years.
articles.body:
The Administrative Office of the US Courts has told Senator Ron Wyden that it will begin tracking how often judges authorize wiretaps carried out with hacking tools and spyware, a category the government calls network investigating techniques. The first tallies will appear in the 2028 Wiretap Report, published in 2029, marking the first public data on a practice the FBI has used since at least 1998.

The statistics will cover cases where spyware is used to intercept real-time communications on encrypted apps such as Signal and WhatsApp. 'The American people remain largely in the dark about the different ways that the government is spying on them,' Wyden said, while urging Congress to pass his Government Surveillance Transparency Act.

Privacy advocates welcomed the change. 'Up until now, we have only been able to guess at the size of the problem,' said Eva Galperin of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, while the ACLU called it an overdue step toward transparency. Italy already publishes similar data, recording 4,321 spyware targets in 2023.

articles.headline: Pixel 11's best new camera trick is a look that ditches the 'smartphone' style
articles.subtitle: Google's Camera Looks process image data at the sensor level to produce photos that don't have the typical smartphone look, with styles such as 'Digi' — but the feature is exclusive to the Pixel 11 series at launch.
articles.body:
Arguably the coolest new photo feature in Google's Pixel 11 lineup is Camera Looks, which processes image data differently at the sensor level to produce photos that don't have that polished 'smartphone' look. The result is styles such as 'Digi', which mimics the aesthetic of photos taken by older digital cameras.

Google says the approach is part of a deliberate shift in its computational photography, trading some of the aggressive processing of recent years for a more natural, film-like rendering. At launch, however, Camera Looks will be exclusive to the Pixel 11 series, which includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL announced at the Made by Google event.

The new lineup brings the usual generational upgrades in cameras, displays and performance, and Google is betting that the distinctive look will be a reason to upgrade. Camera Looks is expected to reach older Pixel phones in a future update.

articles.headline: Stripe will reportedly acquire AI gateway startup OpenRouter for more than $7 billion
articles.subtitle: Bloomberg reports the payments giant is nearing a deal to buy OpenRouter, the platform developers use to route and compare calls to hundreds of AI models, in one of the biggest AI infrastructure acquisitions to date.
articles.body:
Stripe is nearing a deal to acquire OpenRouter, the AI gateway startup that lets developers route API calls across hundreds of models, for more than $7 billion, according to Bloomberg, in a move that would give the payments giant a commanding position in AI infrastructure.

OpenRouter has become a default tool for developers comparing models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and others, and analysts note the acquisition would let Stripe process a growing share of the payments flowing through AI applications. The deal would rank among the largest AI-related acquisitions of the year.

Neither company has commented publicly, and the talks could still fall through, according to the report. The news comes as Stripe is separately reported to be in talks with Advent over a deal for PayPal, in what would be a dramatic reshaping of the payments industry.

articles.headline: Qwen 3.8 27B is excellent — but it defaults to overthinking things
articles.subtitle: Simon Willison's first tests of the new Apache-licensed Alibaba model find it beating its predecessors on benchmarks yet reaching for elaborate reasoning chains even for simple tasks, burning tokens on 20-minute 'thought' sessions.
articles.body:
Qwen 3.8 27B, the latest open-weight model from Alibaba's Qwen lab, is excellent — but it defaults to overthinking, according to Simon Willison, who has been testing it since its release. The 27-billion-parameter model, licensed under Apache 2.0 and capable of understanding images, beats its predecessor Qwen 3.6 27B and even the closed Qwen 3.7-Plus on the lab's self-reported benchmarks.

The catch is that the model defaults to a very high reasoning effort. Willison found it spending 22,276 reasoning tokens — around 20 minutes of thinking — on a simple request to draw a pelican in SVG, running in LM Studio as a 17GB quantized download on an M5 Max MacBook Pro and a DGX Spark.

The 'thinking' can be disabled or tuned, but Willison's verdict is that Qwen's default behavior is a reminder that open models are now competitive with the best closed systems while still being free to run locally. The model card is available on Hugging Face.

articles.headline: Anthropic CEO says AI backlash is 'fundamentally a crisis of trust'
articles.subtitle: Dario Amodei pushes back on claims his risk warnings fueled public distrust, arguing instead that AI companies haven't delivered on their big promises — and that ordinary people suspect the industry is 'cooking up some new way to screw them over'.
articles.body:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has pushed back against the idea that he has painted an overly pessimistic picture of artificial intelligence, arguing instead that the industry's public backlash is 'fundamentally a crisis of trust'. Responding to investor Gavin Baker, who said on the All-In podcast that Amodei's warnings had fueled opposition to AI data centers, Amodei conceded that ordinary people 'don't trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over'.

'I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven't yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world,' he said. 'That is totally on us, and I think it's the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing.'

Amodei also pushed back on the Silicon Valley shorthand that regulation equals regulatory capture, saying many people outside the bubble see regulation as something that constrains corporate power and benefits ordinary people. His comments come as governments on both sides of the Atlantic weigh new rules for the sector.
